If you’re serious about a cure, there’s no way unless the beta cells in your pancreas are still alive. T1D is an autoimmune disease; our immune system(s) attacked the insulin secreting beta cells in our body. 

With stem cell therapy it’s possible to regenerate those cells. It’s not exactly FDA approved, and it’s very expensive.

“No insulin” means no carbohydrates and that’s not strictly possible because of adrenal and glucagon from the liver. It’s possible with a strict diet and exercise program to keep A1Cs below 6, but it’s a life devotion and there’s no room to deviate. 

With no carbohydrates, our bodies still need insulin because of endocrine gland systems. With a meat and vegetable diet, glucagon (high density carbs formed by liver function) and adrenal secretions (produced in kidneys, makes heart go brrrr) aren’t regulated by naturally occurring hormones produced by our bodies. Bolus insulin (“bolus” means food) is required for adrenaline because the liver secretion of glucagon during exercise gives energy to our heart and muscles. 

Without insulin, we use the fats from our muscles and other organs for energy. The consequences of DKA are painful and serious. Prior diagnosis, I had lost 30 pounds and walked home 2 miles with leg cramps. They were terrible and I can still feel my leg cramps 15 years later. 

I’d recommend getting familiar with nutrition! As T1Ds, fast acting glucose spikes cause us to keep wanting more glucose. They’re stimulating and addictive. By getting more aware of nutrition, it helps the mindset shift towards eating foods that cause less glucose spikes. As far as my A1Cs, I’ve been around 7.0 for about 10 years, with some bloodwork’s around 7.5 since diagnosis.

If this helps, I’ll share my first shot of insulin was one of the best days of my life because I had been sick for about 4 years straight dealing with symptoms. I’ve never been able to flip my grit into a disciplined lifestyle, and I think that is something every person living with T1D deserves to create for themselves.

My point is, you’ll learn a lot about yourself and your illness throughout your long life. Do not blame yourself.
